articles.title: The Prem: Sale 28 -24 Harlequins - Late Sharks penalty try wins close game
articles.summary: Harlequins' poor start to the Prem season continues with a third successive loss of the campaign against Sale at CorpAcq Stadium.
articles.body:
Tries: Canakaivata, Warr, Bamber, penalty try Cons: Ford 3

Harlequins' poor start to the Prem season continued with a third successive loss of the campaign against Sale at CorpAcq Stadium.

The Sharks came from behind to win the game with a 73rd-minute penalty try after the returning Marcus Smith had touched down twice in the opening quarter to give Quins an early lead.

After their opening-day reverse to Bristol at home, Sale have bounced back strongly with back-to-back wins over Saracens and Quins.

Despite their first points of the season, the loss leaves Quins rooted to the foot of the table.

Harlequins, crushed 48-0 by Gloucester last weekend, were much more resilient and, with Smith involved for the first time this season after a finger injury, much more threatening.

But Sale, while nowhere near their best, fought their way out of a tight corner to record their fifth successive win against Quins in domestic and European competition.

Quins were good value for a 17-14 half time lead, scoring three tries and having two more disallowed by the television match official (TMO).

Hooker Sam Riley gave them a third-minute lead after Smith and George Furbank had combined in midfield. Then Smith finished off some fine approach play from Furbank.

Sale, without Tom Curry who dropped out through illness, struck back with a try of their own from Fijian Elia Canakaivata on his first Prem start before Smith sliced through some poor defence for his second try.

The hosts cut the deficit just before half-time through scrum-half Gus Warr but with the Sharks making too many errors, Riley was mauled over for Quins' bonus-point try in the 53rd minute.

Sale fought their way back through a try by lock Ben Bamber after a break by Nicky Smith and a big line-out steal from Courtney Lawes kept them within striking distance.

And they went ahead after a rumbling maul which took Quins back 30 metres before Riley pulled the ball down close to the try line.

Referee Christophe Ridley awarded a penalty try and sent the hooker to the sin-bin.

There was no way back for Quins who must hope a change of competition to the Challenge Cup next week, with a home fixture against Vannes, brings a change of fortune.

'I'm really proud of the boys' efforts' - reaction

Harlequins head coach Jason Gilmore told BBC Radio Manchester:

"Fair play to Sale. They got themselves back into the game with their set-piece but I'm really proud of the boys' efforts up here. I'm just happy for the boys that they got some reward out of their work.

"If you're prepared to go to dark places for us and win those collisions, then you're going to get selected. If you're dipping your toe in one week and then not the next, then we can't tolerate that.

"You can't be up one week and then down the next week like we had last week. Performance will dictate the shirts."

Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson said:

"We were chasing the game all day. The fight's in them clearly and it's the second week they've found a way to win.

"They've had to manage the way through games, problem-solve and come up with solutions and that's really rewarding.

"I'm really, really proud of that but we're still not where we want to be in terms of performance because that [chasing the game] won't be good enough against Glasgow next week. We know that - but we'll take this win.

"If you can win playing badly, then that's a good sign. It's up to us to step up, it's all within our hands and our capabilities. That's the exciting bit, isn't it?"

Sale: Carpenter; O'Flaherty, Marchant, Lozowski, Reed; Ford, Warr; N Smith, Jibulu, Opoku-Fordjour, van Rhyn (c), Bamber, Lawes, Tshiunza, Canakaivata.

Replacements: Cowan-Dickie, McIntyre, Francis, Dugdale, Hanson, Louw, Loganimasi.

Harlequins: Furbank; Green, Northmore, Bradley, Murley (c); M Smith, Porter; Hobson, Riley, Kerrod, Dun, Treadwell, Kenningham, Driscoll, Cunningham-South.

Replacements: Walker, Johnson-Holmes, Streeter, Petti, Schmid, Friday, Beard, Isgro.

articles.title: Gallagher Prem: Exeter Chiefs hold on for narrow victory against Newcastle Jets as Sale Sharks edge Harlequins - round-up
articles.summary: Christian Wade scores hat-trick for Newcastle but Exeter Chiefs claim 34-28 win at Sandy Park; Sale Sharks condemn Harlequins to third successive loss at CorpAcq Stadium in Salford
articles.body:
The lead frequently changed hands and it was not until the dying stages that the Chiefs were able to seal victory.

Max Hicks scored Newcastle's other try, with Zack Henry converting all four to secure two valuable bonus points.

Ross Vintcent scored two tries for an error-ridden Exeter, while Sam Harris, Henry Slade and Bachuki Tchumbadze got the others, with Slade converting three and kicking a penalty.

It took Exeter just 40 seconds to open the scoring when Vintcent charged down a clearance kick to gather and score.

Three minutes later Newcastle were level when a long pass from an alert Simon Benitez Cruz gave Wade an easy run-in.

The frenetic opening continued as a well-timed pass from Slade sent Vintcent galloping 20 metres down the right flank to score his second try before skilful handling from the visitors allowed Hicks to cross, with Henry's conversion putting them in front for the first time.

A fifth try arrived before the first quarter had elapsed, with Slade racing through a leaky defence for an individual score, but Exeter then suffered a blow when flanker Ethan Roots was yellow-carded for a no-arms tackle.

Newcastle also suffered a setback when their full-back Harrison Obatoyinbo departed for an HIA, to be replaced by Jake Dalziel, who became the club's youngest ever league debutant aged just 18 years and 54 days.

Dalziel almost made a dream start when his well-judged cross-field kick picked out Werner Kok in acres of space, but a horrible bounce for the wing prevented a certain score.

However, Red Bulls were able to take advantage of Roots' absence when a break from Sammy Arnold provided Wade with his second.

Roots returned from the sin-bin, but Newcastle still led 21-19 at the end of a pulsating first half.

Four minutes after the restart the home side were back in front when a period of pressure was rewarded with the bonus-point try from Harris, on his Prem debut.

However, a handling error from Slade presented Wade with the opportunity to complete his hat-trick, a kick-and-chase securing the touchdown.

Exeter suffered a further blow when Immanuel Feyi-Waboso departed with a leg problem before Red Bulls introduced hooker Samson Adejimi for his debut.

The hosts also made changes by bringing on back-rowers Tom Hooper and Kane James in an attempt to reverse their fortunes and it paid dividends when a Slade penalty gave them a one-point lead before Tchumbadze crashed over to wrap up victory, with Newcastle prop Adam Brocklebank sin-binned.

Harlequins' troubled start to the Gallagher Prem season continued with a third successive loss of the campaign against Sale at CorpAcq Stadium in Salford.

The Sharks left it late but came from behind to snatch a 28-24 success with a 73rd-minute penalty try, after the returning Marcus Smith had touched down twice in the opening quarter to threaten a shock win for the visitors.

After their opening-day reverse to Bristol at home, Sale have bounced back strongly with back-to-back wins over Saracens and Quins.

But despite their first points of the season, the loss leaves Jason Gilmore's team - who suffered their worst league defeat in 26 years last weekend, a 48-0 humbling by Gloucester - rooted to the foot of the table.

With Smith involved for the first time this season after a finger injury, the visitors made seven changes on the back of that embarrassment.

This was a big improvement on that toothless display but, with a late power surge, Sale found a way to chalk up what was their fifth successive win against Harlequins in the league and Europe.

Quins, who had two tries disallowed before the interval, deserved their 17-14 half time lead.

They made a fast start with hooker Sam Riley giving them a third-minute lead, diving over in the corner after Smith and George Furbank had combined in midfield.

Five minutes later Smith was over after a beautiful tip pass from Furbank had freed Luke Northmore down the right wing.

Sale hit back in the 11th minute with a superb try of their own from Fijian number eight Elia Canakaivata on his first Prem start, with Jacques Vermeulen suspended after his red card against Saracens.

Smith went through some weak defence for his second try in the 19th minute and only a brilliant cover tackle from O'Flaherty prevented the England man grabbing his hat-trick inside the first half hour.

Sale cut the deficit two minutes before the break with scrum-half Gus Warr going over after some nice work in midfield from Alex Lozowski.

With the Sharks conceding too many penalties, Riley was mauled over for Quins' bonus-point try in the 53rd minute.

But when Sale finally were able to hold onto possession, second row Ben Bamber crossed after an initial break by Nicky Smith.

Quins pressed again but a crucial lineout steal from Courtney Lawes dug the Sharks out of a hole.

Then Chandler Cunningham-South was unable to find Cadan Murley after intercepting George Ford's pass.

images.caption: Image: Christian Wade's hat-trick was not enough to give Newcastle the win against Exeter

articles.title: Welsh Rugby Union names businessman Lyndon Faulkner as new chair
articles.summary: Lyndon Faulkner, the nephew of Wales legend Charlie Faulkner, will take the role at the WRU's annual general meeting on 22 November.
articles.body:
The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has named former Newport and Ponytpool player Lyndon Faulkner as the governing body's new chairman.

The 66-year-old is the nephew of legendary Wales and Pontypool prop Tony "Charlie" Faulkner and has become a successful businessman in the United States since his playing days.

Faulkner will take over the role vacated by Richard Collier-Keywood at the WRU's annual general meeting on Sunday, 22 November.

He will do so at a time when the WRU is planning to cut the game's professional tier from four to three teams, with west Wales sides Ospreys and Scarlets vying to avoid becoming surplus to requirements.

The WRU has already confirmed the team it owns, Cardiff, and privately-backed Dragons, will continue to exist beyond the 2027-28 season.

The WRU described Faulkner's appointment as "a major coup" and said he can "court the respect of both its community and professional game and the wider business world around it".

WRU publishes data on why west Wales team will be cut

Inside Scarlets and their struggle for existence

Fight for Wales spots heats up as under-threat regions win

In a WRU statement Faulkner said: "This is a pivotal time for the game and I will start by listening to those around me and of course remaining open to credible challenge."

He added: "I know personally how important Welsh rugby is in many different ways to the nation.

"So, it is a huge privilege for me to return to Welsh rugby as chair of the WRU and give something back to a sport which has helped define me and means so much to me, my family, friends and the people of Wales."

The WRU said Faulkner would bring a "fresh perspective" and his mandate, as well as ambassadorial, was to lead strategic direction for the game in Wales and to hold its executive team and staff to account.

WRU chief executive Abi Tierney, who in April 2026 denied Collier-Keywood had been forced out, said: "I know Lyndon and I are ready to form a formidable team working to advance Welsh rugby at all levels."

Faulkner attended Bassaleg Comprehensive School in Newport and played for Newport Youth before going on to figure at centre for their senior side and Pontypool when they were one of Wales' leading teams.

After injury ended his playing days, Faulkner progressed off the field into the corporate world where he has held senior roles including with Technicolor®/Nimbus CD International, Microsoft and Nimbus CD International, Pelican Products and Peli Biothermal.

Faulkner's CV also includes entrepreneur awards and appearing on US TV series 'The Mentor' as well as lecturing at Stanford University Business School and at the University of Virginia's Darden Business School.

articles.title: Prem talking points: Points pile-ups, old-school Saracens and a royal pint
articles.summary: After a try-filled round of action, how high can scoreboard inflation climb and what is behind it?
articles.body:
It is worth taking a step back to fully appreciate the scale of scoring in the Prem currently.

Ten seasons ago Northampton hosted Bath in round three.

As on Saturday, Saints won to end Bath's unbeaten start to the season. The score then was 24-6.

Northampton scored four tries - from Courtney Lawes, George North and David Ribbans (twice). Bath had only two penalties from Rhys Priestland to show for their visit.

This weekend it wasn't just a different game. It was like a different sport.

Between them the teams scored 18 tries en route to a ludicrous 71-48 scoreline.

The 119-point aggregate score was the second highest in English top-flight rugby history, beaten only by Northampton's 94-33 win over Bristol in May.

Those two games are part of a recent trend.

Five of the 10 top-flight games to have breached the 100-point barrier have come since the start of the 2023-24 season.

Looking back at that round of games from 2017-28, there were 26 tries in total across six matches, an average of 4.33 per game.

This weekend there were 50 in five games, an average of 10 per match.

That is an increase on even the first two rounds of this season, which delivered an average of 9.3 tries per game - the highest-scoring start to an English top-flight campaign since data specialists Opta began gathering the statistic in 2007-08.

"The game can be too slanted to attack," Northampton head coach Sam Vesty, whose speciality is attack, told BBC Sport after his side's win.

"I don't want to watch basketball, but we saw some fantastic rugby on both sides."

Vesty believes the current scoring spike is a product of laws of the game and the philosophy of the teams playing it.

"I think officiating [is one factor]," he said.

"The offside line is being reffed hotter; tackle height is lower so therefore people can keep the ball alive more quickly. Then there is the speed of the game - the ball is on a little longer so people are more fatigued.

"I also think there is more intent from teams, going out to score points, when that has not always been the case."

Former England head coach Eddie Jones was always sceptical about how well the Prem prepared players for the grind of Test rugby, where scores are invariably harder earned.

The flip into international action may take some acclimatisation for England's stars this autumn.

It isn't just the throwback kits and spiky presence of Brendan Venter that is giving a retro feeling to Saracens this season.

Defence coach Adam Powell's aim at the start of the season was not just plug some holes, but change the way the game is played in the Prem.

He told his players he wanted Saracens to challenge the dominance of attack and make defence a hallmark of the team, just as it was in their heyday last decade - the Wolfpack reformed.

They have started the season well on that front.

Only Gloucester have conceded fewer points, and keeping previously unbeaten Bristol to just seven points in a 30-7 victory was Saracens' most impressive defensive display of the season.

There was a heft to Sarries' pack with new signing George Martin paired with 6ft 9in prospect Olamide Sodeke in the second row and Maro Itoje, looking revitalised after his summer break, impressing at blind-side flanker.

Owen Farrell piloted the hosts well from fly-half, bringing his accuracy as well as his usual intensity.

Saracens' most destructive defensive force at home, though, might go unseen.

Bristol rested three players - Pedro Rubiolo, AJ MacGinty and Steven Luatua – because of concerns about their bodies , external holding up to playing on the artificial surface at the Stonex Stadium.

The Bears are not the only club who will avoid selecting players , external with particular injury histories on artificial surfaces.

With Newcastle's pitch having been relaid over the summer, and Gloucester's first put down in 2021, Saracens' surface is now the oldest of its type in the Prem.

It may be the one area where Saracens will look to the future soon.

After starting Northampton's first two games of the season, scrum-half Archie McParland had a bench role in the win over Bath.

The 21-year-old, who would have toured with England this summer but for lacerated leg suffered in the Prem final win over Exeter, got on for the final 20 minutes against Bath.

Meanwhile, 22-year-old Charlie Bracken got 40 minutes on his first start of the season for Saracens in their win over Bristol, providing speedy service and aiming some well-judged bombs for brother Jack to chase.

However, both McParland and Bracken face formidable roadblocks in the way of more regular game time in the Prem.

British and Irish Lions Alex Mitchell and Tomos Williams are their respective team-mates at Saints and Sarries.

How will their clubs manage their resources at nine? Is it possible to keep everyone happy? Does 20-year-old Lucas Friday, who signed a new contract at Harlequins last month and may see a clearer route into the first team, have an advantage?

It will be intriguing to see how the next generation of England nines plays out.

Early signs of a more competitive campaign

After a round in which three of the five games finished within a winning margin of seven or fewer points, there is not one unbeaten side in the league.

It is still early days. The form lines are still murky.

Sale, who saw off Harlequins 28-24 on Sunday, are particularly difficult to pick as their new combinations and more expansive gameplan coalesce.

If they come good, you could see any of the top eight sides contending for the play-offs.

In the first season with a salary floor as well as a salary cap, it feels like a tighter, more competitive tournament after some chasms in the table last time round.

A few entertaining snippets you may have missed...

Full-back George Furbank's quicksilver hands , external drawing a gasp in Harlequins' much-improved performance.

After his round-one antics , more footballing brilliance and nimble footwork , external from Bath full-back Santi Carreras.

Newcastle Red Bulls wing Werner Kok's circus skills warm-up. , external

The Duke of Sussex taking in Leicester's win over Gloucester in the Ed Slater Cup, plastic pint pot in hand.

Image caption, Charlie and Jack Bracken are the sons of former Saracens and England scrum-half Kyran
Image caption, Prince Harry (right) watches Leicester play Gloucester

articles.title: Leeds Rhinos, St Helens, Hull KR, Hull FC release statements in support of NRL investment after Leigh Leopards owner comes out against deal
articles.summary: A vote on a partnership between the National Rugby League (NRL) and Super League is close; it is understood the NRL would want to increase Super League to 15 teams and add London Broncos into the competition for 2027
articles.body:
Talks have been ongoing for months regarding the Australian competition's potential future involvement in Super League to bring alignment between the top two rugby league competitions in the world.

As a requirement of the deal, it is understood the NRL would want London Broncos added to the top flight as the 15th team from the 2027 season onwards which has been a potential sticking point for some clubs, with Leigh Leopards owner Derek Beaumont taking to social media to say he is against the deal because of that particular point.

Beaumont said it is "just not right to put London in Super League".

The Leigh owner's particular grievance is that London finished 16th in the gradings, outside of the automatic Super League spots.

Not only that, if they were to be added to Super League, he would want a similar process to take place to the one that saw Toulouse Olympique and York Knights elevated in 2026. Their applications went through an independent panel.

However, other clubs see the partnership as a "landmark" and "defining" moment for the sport.

A deadline for the deal to go through is reportedly at the end of this week at which clubs will vote on whether they want the partnership to take place.

Beaumont said on Sunday that he would vote against the deal. Since then, Leeds, St Helens and both Hull clubs have released statements to confirm they are in favour of the partnership, the two Hull teams releasing a symbolic joint statement in a show of solidarity between the city rivals.

Leeds owner Paul Caddick said "Leeds Rhinos and the Caddick Group give their wholehearted support to a working arrangement between the Super League and NRL and I believe this will be a gamechanger for the sport in this country".

St Helens then followed to say they "reaffirm their long-standing support for a strategic partnership as part of an exciting plan to globalise the sport".

The joint statement between Hull KR and Hull FC then followed, in which they "confirmed their united support for a proposed strategic partnership between Super League and Australia's National Rugby League, in what could represent a defining moment for the future of rugby league in the northern hemisphere".

articles.title: Totoa Auvaa: Saracens academy player sacked after incident in St Albans
articles.summary: Saracens sack Totoa Auvaa, the academy player who was involved in a nightclub incident with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson, after another incident.
articles.body:
Saracens have sacked Totoa Auvaa, the academy player who was involved in a nightclub incident with England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson in June.

The English Prem club have confirmed that the 21-year-old Samoan forward has left with immediate effect following another incident in St Albans on Saturday.

Auvaa had originally been stood down from all club duties while Saracens investigated the matter.

"The club has determined that his conduct falls short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch," read a club statement. , external

"We take our responsibilities to our supporters, young people and partners seriously and we remain committed to upholding the standards of our conduct expected across the club."

A disciplinary hearing by the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) found that then England captain Stokes and pace bowler Atkinson breached "contractual obligations" but were blameless for "violent conduct" in an incident in June.

Both were present in a London nightclub when a member of England's security staff was left bloodied and in need of medical attention after being struck by Auvaa.

Stokes and Atkinson were made unavailable for England's second Test defeat by New Zealand while Auvaa was not sanctioned.

All-rounder Stokes was restored to the team for the deciding third Test, during which he made a stunning announcement to retire from international cricket at the conclusion of the match.

images.caption: Image caption, Totoa Auvaa is a Samoan back row

articles.title: Totoa Auvaa: Saracens sack academy forward involved in nightclub fracas with Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson after new incident
articles.summary: Saracens have dismissed Senior Men’s Academy forward Totoa Auvaa with immediate effect following an incident at the weekend; the 21-year-old Samoan was part of the June nightclub altercation that preceded Ben Stokes’ retirement from international cricket
articles.body:
The 21-year-old Samoan, a member of the club's Senior Men's Academy, was involved in an incident in St Albans on Saturday night.

Saracens confirmed on Monday evening Auvaa had left the club following an internal investigation.

"Saracens can confirm that Totoa Auvaa, a member of the Senior Men's Academy, has left the club with immediate effect," a club statement said.

"Following an incident this weekend, the club has determined that his conduct falls short of the standards expected of everyone who represents Saracens, both on and off the pitch.

"We take our responsibilities to our supporters, young people and partners seriously and we remain committed to upholding the standards of our conduct expected across the club.

"We will not be making any further comment on this matter."

Auvaa escaped punishment following the nightclub incident in June which led to cricketers Stokes and Gus Atkinson being dropped by England for the second Test against New Zealand.

Saracens called the events "regrettable" while describing themselves as "supportive" of the player.

Separate Saracens and England cricket nights out had converged on two pubs before Stokes, Atkinson and Auvaa ended up in the VIP area of the Rex Rooms nightclub in the early hours of Monday June 8.

The two players had broken a midnight curfew while celebrating a first Test win over New Zealand at Lord's and both were dropped for the second Test.

An England and Wales Cricket Board investigation cleared Stokes and Atkinson of violent conduct, finding they had been blameless victims of "unprovoked attacks".

Stokes and Atkinson were given formal written warnings for breaching their central contracts before returning for the third Test at Trent Bridge, where Stokes resigned the captaincy and announced his retirement from international cricket .

Atkinson has remained in the England set-up and has since been awarded another central contract.

articles.title: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: Mikey Lewis out for England opener
articles.summary: Harry Smith is named alongside captain George Williams in the England half-back roles for their 2026 Rugby League World Cup opening match against Tonga - with Mikey Lewis left out.
articles.body:
Harry Smith has been named alongside captain George Williams in England's half-back roles for their Rugby League World Cup opening match against Tonga - with Mikey Lewis left out.

Lewis, who pipped 2025 Super League Man Of Steel Jake Connor to a place in England's squad, has not even made the bench for Saturday's fixture.

Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent year, did enough to convince England head coach Brian McDermott that he should join captain Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Smith as half-back options.

But he will be one of three players, along with Ben Currie and Ben Talty, listed as non-playing reserves.

England face Tonga in Perth on Saturday (10:05 BST), before taking on France in the same city on 24 October and then Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on 30 October.

England men: AJ Brimson, Dom Young, Hugo Savala, Herbie Farnworth, Zach Eckersley, George Williams, Harry Smith, Max King, Brad O'Neill, Morgan Knowles, Junior Nsemba, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley.

Interchange: Jez Litten, Luke Thompson, Ethan Havard, Sam Walters, Jack Welsby, Matty Ashton.

Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad

Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad

McDermott, who succeeded Shaun Wane in April, has also made a major selection call at full-back.

AJ Brimson has been chosen ahead of Jack Welsby in the key role for England's first game in Group B-C - a combined pool of six teams, from which the top two will go through to the semi-finals early next month.

McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad.

And Brisbane-born Brimson - who made his England debut in last year's Ashes series against Australia - is one of four such players in the squad, alongside England debutant Max King.

Bulldogs prop King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, features alongside fellow debutant Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad. Victor Radley is also in the XIII.

All of the men's and women's teams for the first round of matches between Thursday and Sunday were announced on Tuesday at 06:00 BST.

England women's coach Stu Barrow named his squad for their opener against Wales on Saturday in Perth (07:35 BST).

Jasmin Strange and Connie Boyd will make their international debuts, while uncapped Hope Millard is among the interchanges.

Opponents Wales will give a debut to second-row forward Paige Travis - who played for England at the last World Cup four years ago.

Tayla Preston - who captains Canterbury Bulldogs in the NRL Women's Premiership - will start at scrum-half, with former rugby union international Ffion Lewis alongside her at stand-off, while Hannah Bluck will represent Wales at a fourth different sport.

Bluck has won senior Wales honours in rugby union as well as gaining junior rank recognition in football and basketball.

England women: Fran Goldthorp, Anna Davies, Georgia Wilson, Connie Boyd, Amelia Brown, Isabel Rowe, Georgia Roche, Mary Coleman, Keara Bennett, Hollie-Mae Dodd, Jasmin Strange, Eva Hunter, Megan Williams.

Interchange: Jodie Cunningham, Vicky Whitfield, Jenna Foubister, Hope Millard.

Wales women: Leanne Burnell, Dani McGifford, Hannah Bluck, Zoe Heeley, Frances Layton, Ffion Lewis, Tayla Preston, Agnes Wood, Jasmine Gibbons, Emily Hughes, Georgia Cussons, Paige Travis, Bethan Dainton.

Interchange: Carys Marsh, Kathryn Salter, Katie Carr, Erin Williams.

Walsh pips Tedesco to Australia full-back role

Reece Walsh has been selected ahead of James Tedesco at full-back for Australia - co-hosts and men's World Cup favourites - as they face New Zealand in the tournament's opening match on Thursday (10:05 BST).

Walsh was the star player in Australia's 3-0 Ashes series whitewash of England last year, but has endured a tougher 2026.

Injury has prevented Walsh from playing since August 15, while Tedesco won the Clive Churchill medal for best player in the 2026 Australian National Rugby League Grand Final.

But head coach Kevin Walters has stuck with Walsh in a backline that includes Test debutant Jack Bostock on one wing and Tom Trbojevic on the other.

Loose forward Isaah Yeo has delayed surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to captain Australia.

But star half-back Nathan Cleary is out of the tournament with a broken ankle.

Australia men: Reece Walsh, Jack Bostock, Latrell Mitchell, Kotoni Staggs, Tom Trbojevic, Cameron Munster, Mitchell Moses, Patrick Carrigan, Harry Grant, Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, Jacob Preston, Liam Martin, Isaah Yeo

Interchanges: Tom Dearden, Cameron Murray, Reuben Cotter, Keaon Koloamatangi, David Fifita, Bradman Best

articles.title: Baxter hopes to bring Exeter fans back to Sandy Park
articles.summary: Exeter boss Rob Baxter says he will do what he can to create a side that can bring crowds back to Sandy Park.
articles.body:
Exeter Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter says he will do what he can to create a side that can bring crowds back to Sandy Park.

The club closed their North Terrace for the first time for a league fixture in Sunday's 34-28 win over Newcastle.

A crowd of just 7,071 attended the game at the 15,600-capacity home of last season's beaten Prem finalists, despite the club cutting ticket prices earlier this month.

It led to an at times eerily quiet atmosphere at a ground that is normally noisy, especially for a league game.

The attendance lower than the 8,682 present for Exeter's first home league game of the season against Gloucester last month - their first competitive game since being beaten by Northampton at Twickenham in June.

"The job I have to do to help build the crowd is to make sure the team perform well and win games of rugby," Baxter told BBC Sport.

"Today we probably didn't perform quite well enough, but having said that it did mean there was a game that had jeopardy in it right until the final whistle, so anybody here supporting it should have had a great entertaining day.

"They may have looked and gone 'oh, I want it to be comfortable', but actually they've stayed until the last second because the game was still in the balance, so we've ticked that box.

"When you have a fairly poor crowd there are things off the field that you have to address and look at as well.

"They are ongoing and I know a lot of people looking into those things."

Having had a club-record worst season in the top flight in 2024-25, Exeter rallied last season to finish fourth last season before beating Bath at the Rec in the Prem semi-finals.

The club was taken over by Black Knight Rugby - part of the same American investment group that owns Premier League football side AFC Bournemouth - earlier this year.

On Monday 12 October, tickets for Exeter's next home league game in the Prem against Harlequins on 31 October were on sale for between £75 and £97 in the West Grandstand, while seats in the opposite East Stand cost between £35 and £87.

Seats for the same game behind the in-goal area in the east of the ground cost from £10 for children to between £35 and £45 for an adult while standing prices around the ground for an adult go from £24.50 to as much as £55 for the most desirable area by the halfway line in the East Terrace.

Tickets are cheaper for Exeter's two Prem Rugby Cup matches in November while chief executive Tony Rowe says prices will be reduced for more games before Christmas.

"The South West is full of hard-working people who live in a region where house prices are high and salaries do not allow for generous disposable incomes," he said in a statement on the club website.

"We have made the decision to cut the price of some ticket categories for our league, European and cup games up to Christmas to thank our fans for their support in September and to ease the pressure on people's pockets.

"The biggest reductions are on children and youth tickets to help fans with families."

articles.title: Jacob Stockdale: Tears, family and 'being boring' - Ulster wing's milestone moment
articles.summary: After he made a milestone 150th appearance for Ulster on Satruday, Jacob Stockdale tells BBC Sport NI about his tears, family and being "unbelievably boring" about Ireland.
articles.body:
Jacob Stockdale had run out of the tunnel wearing the Ulster jersey many times before - 149, to be exact.

With his daughters, Phoebe and Bonnie, either side of him, he was the first player out on the pitch against Munster as he marked a century-and-a-half of Ulster appearances.

It had been a long time coming for a wing who burst onto the scene in 2016, only for injuries to derail so much early promise.

But, after a resurgent few years, he was thankful to reach the milestone with his family by his side.

"When I was walking out, I was like, 'I'm going to cry here'," he told BBC Sport NI.

"I had to kind of pull it back a wee bit a couple of times. My family are incredibly important to me and it was a very emotional day."

Ulster playing games like training sessions - Murphy

Ulster fight back to draw with Munster in thriller

Stockdale's landmark moment came a week later than scheduled after he was forced out of the team to face Glasgow in the warm-up, but to do it at home, against your Irish rivals and with his family there, made it even more special.

The 30-year-old said it was "an amazing experience" to reach 150 games in white and red.

"When you get your first cap here, you dream about those days and to get to do it with my two daughters was amazing.

"Those are the memories you hold on to after you're long gone from the pitch. It was really special."

His first try came in the first half as he beat two Munster players to touch down, and his second came in Ulster's comeback as he finished off a fine, flowing move.

"I always hoped I would [reach 150 Ulster appearances].

"I figured when I started playing here, that if I kept doing my job well and kept performing, that I'd maybe be able to reach it.

"But it was throughout the last week, looking back over the years, it was a bit of a pinch me moment, but it's been brilliant."

Stockdale marked his milestone occasion with two tries in Belfast, but not the win he had hoped for.

A week on from a 33-33 draw in Glasgow, Ulster fought back from being 21 points down at half-time but had to settle for another thrilling draw with their Irish rivals.

It means that Richie Murphy's side are without a win in their opening three United Rugby Championship matches, and Ulster's head coach had said his side were "playing matches like they are training sessions".

"You can't do anything else than be honest and be up front," Stockdale said.

"There's no point in sugarcoating anything because that doesn't help you get better.

"For us, it's making sure that we're process-driven and not trying to focus too much on the outcomes."

Ulster are back in action on Saturday as Murphy's side travel to Zebre in the Challenge Cup.

Stockdale was key as Ulster reached the final of last season's competition, where they were convincingly beaten by Montpellier in the sweltering Bilbao heat to miss out on a first trophy in 20 years.

The wing missed the final with a fractured cheek picked up in the win over Exeter Chiefs in the last four, and he says "we're all still hurting a bit" from defeat in the decider.

"Equally, we saw what we were capable of in the cup last year," he said.

"It's just about putting those performances back on the pitch and I don't see any reason why we can't push on and do what we did last year, and hopefully more."

As is often the case, the topic of Ireland selection comes up with the Rugby World Cup now less than 12 months away.

When he burst onto the scene with his Ireland debut, with 19 tries in his first four years as an international, it looked like he would be a fixture on Ireland's wing for years to come.

But, injuries and a resulting loss of form saw him drop out of the international picture.

However, he has worked himself back into the frame and was involved in Ireland's Nations Championship, with four more November fixtures to come.

It was fitting that his two tries on his landmark appearance for Ulster came in front of Ireland head coach Andy Farrell - something Stockdale did not realise at the time.

But it is something that doesn't phase him, regardless of who is in the stands.

In short, "it's something I can't control", so his full focus is on his performances in white.

"I know that's a bit of a cliche answer that everybody says, but I'm just worrying about my rugby here and whatever else happens, happens.

"I'm really not going to worry about it. I'm just worrying about my rugby here."

He is asked again but his Ireland prospects in a big year, but he's happy to be "unbelievably boring again".

"Genuinely, I'm just worried about the next couple of weeks with Ulster.

"I'm looking forward to the Zebre game, going after it and then it will be the Bulls and Stormers.

"Anything else that comes in a month's time or a year's time, I'll worry about it then."

Image caption, Stockdale marked his 150th Ulster appearance with two tries against Munster
Image caption, Stockdale is back in the Ireland picture after an injury-hit few years

articles.title: Castleford Tigers: Ex-St Helens boss Paul Rowley named new head coach
articles.summary: Paul Rowley takes over as Castleford Tigers head coach, with the former St Helens boss signing a three-year contract.
articles.body:
Castleford Tigers have appointed Paul Rowley as their head coach on a three-year contract.

Rowley had been out of work since leaving St Helens in July, halfway through his first season in charge.

The Tigers had been without a head coach following the departure of Australian Ryan Carr in August for personal reasons.

Castleford finished second bottom in Super League with only eight wins from their 27 games, but received an A score in the IMG ratings released last week.

The Tigers will be the third Super League club Rowley has been in charge of after Salford Red Devils and then Saints.

He led Salford into the play-offs in 2022 and 2024, playing an exciting style of rugby before severe financial issues took over and he eventually left the club.

It landed him the job at St Helens, but after an injury-hit difficult spell, he departed with the club sixth in the table , with Saints eventually missing out on the play-offs.

He now moves over to West Yorkshire, and a Castleford team who have not reached the play-offs since 2019 and have just seen local rivals Wakefield Trinity win the Grand Final.

Cas were only kept off the bottom of Super League by Bradford Bulls, with the club hoping he can be the man to rejuvenate them.

"Paul has a proven track record of building competitive teams, developing players and creating an attacking brand of rugby that supporters can get behind," said Castleford director of rugby Chris Chester.

"He has a real passion for the game, strong leadership qualities and a clear vision of how he wants his teams to play."

Can Rowley bring back 'Classy Cas' style?

It hasn't taken long for Paul Rowley's enthusiasm for rugby league to get the better of him and put him right back in the hurly-burly world of Super League with Castleford.

In fairness, there's been plenty of time for the 51-year-old to refresh his mind between standing down as coach at St Helens and the official, formal release which occurred a few weeks ago.

He's got plenty to do with Cas too, so no time like the present to get stuck in and mastermind the kind of team-building job he managed so impressively before at Leigh, Toronto and Salford.

Incoming NRL imports like Damien Cook, Mat Feagai and Tyrell Sloan will certainly help in that, as will Robbie Mulhern to beef up the pack, while Rowley's close relationship with director of rugby Chris Chester from their Halifax days could also be a crucial factor.

There was a fair list of departures at the end of last season so there is possibly wriggle room in terms of bringing people in.

Traditionally, Rowley's teams have been renowned for a varied and entertaining attacking style, and with 'Classy Cas' the mantra at Wheldon Road, in theory it's an ideal fit.

Rowley certainly did not become a bad coach overnight after he was unable to complete the job at Saints.

Cas fans will hope for a similar result to rivals Wakefield, who have soared to success since appointing Daryl Powell after his similarly unfruitful time at Warrington.

images.caption: Image caption, Paul Rowley lost six out of 10 games before leaving St Helens in July

articles.title: Louis Rees-Zammit: Wales and Bristol wing calls for the end of use of artificial pitches
articles.summary: Wales and Bristol star Louis Rees-Zammit calls for the end of artificial playing surfaces in top-flight rugby.
articles.body:
Wales and Bristol star Louis Rees-Zammit has called for an end to artificial playing surfaces in top-flight rugby.

Rees-Zammit played in the Bears' 30-7 defeat by Saracens on Saturday at the StoneX Stadium, and posted a picture on social media showing a heavily scarred right leg.

Prem clubs Saracens, Gloucester and Newcastle all play on artificial pitches, with the state of the Sarries surface coming under scrutiny this season.

Rees-Zammit posted the photo with the caption: "Can we please stop playing on these Astroturf pitches!! Someone do something about it!!"

Meanwhile, it emerged over the weekend that Bristol director of rugby Pat Lam did not select three of his key players because of the state of the pitch in north London.

Pedro Rubiolo, AJ MacGinty and Steven Luatua were rested for the trip to north London.

"They came off big injuries last season so it wasn't worth putting them on that pitch," Lam explained.

"If we were playing the game at home or if it was a semi-final, they would have played."

Points pile-ups, old-school Saracens and a royal pint - Prem talking points

Saracens sack academy player Auvaa after latest incident

Caluori scores as Saracens too strong for Bristol

In response, Saracens chief executive Ed Coetzee says the surface is kept under "constant review" and meets all maintenance and safety criteria.

"Following recent comments about the pitch at StoneX Stadium, here are the facts," Coetzee said.

"The surface holds a valid World Rugby Regulation 22 certificate until 1 April 2028. Our SF4 documentation was with Prem Rugby ahead of the deadline. The maintenance programme is followed to the letter. We take pitch condition and player welfare seriously, and we keep the surface under constant review.

"Certified, submitted and maintained. Anyone who would like to see the paperwork only has to ask.

"Who an opposition club picks is entirely its own business and we'd prefer our pitch to be remembered for the rugby played on it, rather than the excuses made afterwards."

images.caption: Image caption, Louis Rees-Zammit played in Bristol's defeat at Saracens, who play on an artificial pitch

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: What represents success for England & home nations?
articles.summary: Some teams have their eyes on a trophy - others are prioritising longer-term gains. BBC Sport assesses a Rugby League World Cup that comes at a pivotal time for the international game.
articles.body:
"Do I believe we can win? It's not a no. Anybody who says we can't win with a finality to it - that's not my belief."

England's new men's head coach Brian McDermott has sounded a note of hope going into the Rugby League World Cup. And he is not the only coach looking forward with optimism. For now at least, everybody harbours a dream.

Not everyone taking part in the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments over the next month is expecting to come away with a winner's medal - but they all have a target for success. For some, it's a title. For others, it's showing progress, or creating a legacy.

The men's competition kicks off first, on Thursday (10:05 BST), with reigning champions Australia facing New Zealand in a Sydney blockbuster dubbed a potential dress rehearsal for the final.

Both will certainly have their sights on lifting the trophy in Brisbane on 15 November.

It is a similar story for Australia's women - seeking a fourth successive title - as they begin their campaign against Samoa in Sydney on Friday (10:05 BST).

England, meanwhile, have high hopes of retaining their wheelchair title - they start against Wales in Wollongong on Friday, 30 October (04:30 BST).

Australia is hosting the bulk of the the three tournaments - including all of the wheelchair matches - with Papua New Guinea staging two men's and two women's games and New Zealand one of each.

Here, BBC Sport examines what would represent success at this World Cup for England, the home nations and the tournament as a whole.

Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand

Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

Lewis left out for England's Rugby League World Cup opener

McDermott bids to reignite England men's hopes

Four years ago, England's men suffered a gut-wrenching 27-26 golden-point World Cup semi-final defeat by Samoa at Emirates Stadium.

Series wins over Tonga in 2023 and Samoa a year later banished some of those memories - but last autumn brought a 3-0 home series loss to Australia.

The manner of that defeat led to Shaun Wane's departure and a new head coach in McDermott, who is seeking to lead England to only their second final since 1995.

However, prior to his squad's arrival Down Under last week, the Gold Coast Titans assistant had not even had the benefit of a training session with his players.

There was no mid-season international this year to help England prepare for a World Cup programme that begins on Saturday against a powerful Tonga side packed with NRL talent.

England then take on France and Papua New Guinea in Pool B-C - a combined six-team group from which the top two will reach the semi-finals.

Yet despite limited preparation opportunities, England will have hope of reaching a fourth final if they find their rhythm.

McDermott's 23-man squad boasts arguably the best centre in the world in Dolphins star Herbie Farnworth, while lock Victor Radley has just helped Sydney Roosters win the Grand Final in Australia.

They are two of 10 NRL-based players selected by the former Leeds boss, who has taken advantage of utilising heritage players to call up versatile Roosters back Hugo Savala and Brisbane Broncos front-rower Ben Talty.

Huddersfield-born Canterbury Bulldogs prop Max King, who has previously appeared for New South Wales in State of Origin, will also make his bow, and with Harry Smith among seven Wigan players in contention, there will be no shortage of big-game experience in England's ranks.

While England showed plenty of passion and physicality against Australia in 2025, McDermott has emphasised that more guile is required in attack.

"We have got to do things differently," McDermott said.

"Being passionate to play for England is huge. You have to be aggressive to play our game, you have to be a warrior, a gladiator - but you have to have some smart attack as well.

"You have to play with a point of difference and attack into certain areas. I don't believe too many England teams have done that over the years."

Smith, who helped Wigan defeat Penrith in World Club Challenge in 2024, added that McDermott has shown the players how he wants them to be more positive.

"He's showed us clips from the Ashes series, where there were opportunities to go at Australia," Smith said.

"Big opportunities to break open the game which we didn't quite grab. [It's] Probably just a bit more eyes up, a bit more playing on the gainline.

"In big games, you've got to take your chances with two hands and come away with points."

The women using up annual leave for a World Cup dream

England's women, ranked third in the world, travel to Australia with memories still fresh of their record 90-4 defeat by the Jillaroos in Las Vegas in March 2025.

They will meet again at this World Cup - a Group A fixture against the world champions is bookended by matches against Wales and a showdown with Samoa in Wollongong that could determine whether they reach the last four for the fifth time.

The complexion of Stuart Barrow's squad has altered dramatically - a youthful and dynamic squad features only six of the team who featured in Nevada.

It is buoyed by the inclusion of Australia-born Jasmin Strange, with the Sydney Roosters second-row forward joined by another heritage player - Hope Millard of Canterbury Bulldogs.

Barrow's squad is also enhanced by the return of Australia-based Fran Goldthorp, Georgia Roche and Hollie-Mae Dodd.

St Helens' loose forward Jodie Cunningham, 34, provides valuable experience in her fourth and final World Cup. The new headline acts include a Wigan trio - 19-year-old Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister, Megan Williams and Eva Hunter.

"It's a huge difference in a short period of time. The result [against Australia] enhanced the desire to make change. We have lots of youth and enthusiasm," said Cunningham.

"As a squad we are probably going to be underestimated by Australia and other nations whose players predominantly play in the NRLW - and Eva [Hunter] could be one that does shock them with her physicality. She is so strong, powerful and really quick with it as well.

"Maybe that's the benefit of that scoreline in Vegas - people won't realise the talent we've got."

As in the NRL Women's Premiership (NRLW), matches at the Women's Rugby League World Cup with be played over 70 minutes, rather than 80, as it is in the Women's Super League.

Despite the improvement in standards that Women's Super League has driven, Barrow's side face an enormous task in competing with New Zealand and Australia - the only two nations to have lifted the trophy in six previous World Cups.

Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad

Players from those nations feature almost exclusively in the professional NRLW.

In contrast, the majority of the England squad have full-time jobs - as was the case four years ago.

"I know some of the girls have had to take all of their annual leave for the tournament, so they've not had a holiday all year because they've been saving it up," Leeds hooker Keara Bennett told BBC Sport.

"I think the more time we've got to invest into our training, into recovery, it just allows us to be better players and a better team.

"We're trying to create a platform and inspire the next generation, but you can't not acknowledge that money and time would really benefit and boost us."

Wigan scrum-half Isabel Rowe added: "It's definitely a struggle we have trying to make sure everybody's free and available to play.

"I don't like to use the word 'sacrifice' because we're making a choice and we choose to do it because we want to play for our country, but you have to take it into account."

'My goal in life is to create moments and memories'

England head into the wheelchair competition looking for their third title and will expect to advance from a group containing Wales, the USA and Ireland.

Head coach Tom Coyd has included five World Cup winners in his 10-player squad and the aim is simple - to replicate their triumph in 2022.

"We're going there with the attitude that we want to win," said Luis Domingos, who is one of two Sheffield Eagles players featuring.

"My goal in life is to create moments and memories, and to leave a mark. I'm confident we can win but I'm more excited about creating that memory that I can remember in 20 years.

"Me and my family - the team-mates and the staff - can create that moment, and the next generation can say: I want to do something like that."

Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad

Wales make their bow in the women's competition after progressing through qualifying but will be rank outsiders in a group containing Australia, Samoa and England, who beat them 82-0 at Headingley in 2024, and 62-0 in Neath last year.

Tom Brindle has named three players who turned out in Wales' first-ever game in 2021 against England - Leanne Burnell, Kathryn Salter and Emily Hughes.

The squad is supplemented by North Queensland Cowboys winger Sian Williams, second rower Paige Travis - who has switched allegiances from England - and Canterbury Bulldogs half-back Tayla Preston.

"My grandfather was born in Wales and grew up in Wales before moving here when he was about 20," Preston said.

"I feel really honoured to be able to play for Wales in a World Cup, and hopefully we can help grow the game for girls back in Wales and inspire them to want to play."

Most of those in the Wales ranks are taking unpaid leave to play, while the Welsh wheelchair squad raised over £10,000 via crowdfunding to help pay for costs after they lost their front-of-shirt sponsor at short notice.

Ireland and Scotland will join Wales and England at the wheelchair tournament.

While Ireland were beaten in every match in the wheelchair event four years ago, they have subsequently climbed to third in the world rankings.

And a squad containing Wigan quartet Oran Spain, Toby Burton-Carter, Mel Griffith and player-coach Phil Roberts will look to reach at least the semi-finals.

Meanwhile, Scotland face a huge challenge in a group containing France - the runners-up in 2022 - and a powerhouse Australia team who ran England close in two Tests last autumn.

But they do have a World Cup winner in their ranks. James Simpson-Hill - who helped England to victory four years ago - came out of retirement earlier this year and has switched to the nation where his father was born.

Bluck earns Rugby League World Cup call from Wales

While newer rugby league nations such as Greece and Jamaica delivered a feelgood factor at the last World Cup, the men's tournament has been trimmed from 16 teams to 10 this time to reduce the number of lopsided group matches. The women's and wheelchair tournaments have both stuck with eight teams.

Familiar issues remain around the health of the game, including the levels of finance it can generate commercially and the space for an international calendar.

England's men have played just nine matches since 2022, with two of those being high-scoring and rather uncompetitive wins over France.

It is a similar same story for the Kangaroos - the sport's most successful international side - who were without a Test fixture for almost three years prior to their arrival in England in 2022 and have only had nine since.

Plans to spread the gospel of the game further by staging the tournament in the US and Canada in 2025 had to be shelved because of financial concerns and French organisers then pulled out before the International Rugby League shifted it back a year and moved it to the southern hemisphere.

With Australia's men and women the overwhelming favourites to triumph, organisers face an ongoing challenge to deliver a competitive and profitable World Cup that helps grow the game.

"I don't think the future of the game rests on this World Cup," added McDermott.

"If England win the World Cup, it'd be good. But does that mean Sky is going to treble the money that they give the clubs? The answer is no.

"And the answer would be, you know, growing the game. It's a long term [thing]. [We need to] Get in better and more sustainable investment, and there are a few more things that the game needs to do."

articles.title: Lawrence Dallaglio: 2003 World Cup winner's medal sells for £54K at auction
articles.summary: Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio's 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal is sold for £54,000 at auction.
articles.body:
Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio's 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal has been sold for £54,000 at auction.

The 54-year-old put a number of items from his illustrious career up for sale, including medals, trophies and caps, after being declared bankrupt.

A British and Irish Lions cap was sold for £11,000, an England cap for £8,000 and a 2003 Six Nations Championship winner's medal for £7,500.

A number of items went unsold, including Dallaglio's medals for his four Premiership title wins with Wasps.

Dallaglio's collection had an estimated value of £180,000, with the items sold raising £100,500 in the auction at Budd's in Northamptonshire , external .

He was one of the key members of the England squad that won the World Cup in dramatic fashion against Australia 23 years ago.

During an appearance on The High Performance Podcast , external earlier this month, Dallaglio spoke about his bankruptcy.

He said: "As a result of getting divorced, I was made bankrupt. I had some financial problems - I could've done things a lot better."

He also said he sought therapy after his divorce and bankruptcy left him wallowing in "self-pity".

images.caption: Image caption, Lawrence Dallaglio played at number eight for England in the 2003 Rugby World Cup final against Australia
